Where is Norfolk, Virginia, and how big is it?

Norfolk is an independent city in the southeastern corner of Virginia, where the Elizabeth River meets the Chesapeake Bay. It is not part of any county, so the city handles its own assessments, tax billing and zoning.

The city covers 96.41 square miles, but only 53.28 of those are land. The other 43.13 square miles are water, and the average elevation is about 6.9 feet. The 2020 census counted 238,005 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 231,013.

Norfolk sits at the center of Hampton Roads, a metro area of more than 1.8 million people. Virginia Beach and Chesapeake are larger by population, which makes Norfolk the third-largest city in the region and fourth in the state.

How did Norfolk grow into the city it is today?

Norfolk began as a colonial seaport in the late 1600s and received a royal borough charter in 1736. It was incorporated as a city in 1845.

The Navy shaped the modern city. The 1907 Jamestown Exposition at Sewell's Point led to a naval air station in 1917, which became Naval Station Norfolk, the largest naval base in the world.

The city also grew by annexation. It took in Berkley in 1906, then Sewell's Point, Willoughby Spit, Campostella and Ocean View in 1923. Later annexations in 1955 and 1959, plus a 1988 land swap with Virginia Beach, set today's borders.

Highway building changed where people lived. The Downtown Tunnel opened in 1952, the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel in 1957, the Midtown Tunnel in 1962 and the Virginia Beach-Norfolk Expressway in 1967. Those links helped suburbs form and pulled residents out of older neighborhoods.

Which Norfolk neighborhoods do sellers hear about most?

Norfolk has dozens of named neighborhoods, and the age and style of the houses change from one to the next. These are the ones that Wikipedia singles out.

  • Freemason and West Freemason: historic downtown neighborhoods with some of the oldest buildings in the city.
  • Berkley: a former separate city, annexed in 1906 and located across the Elizabeth River.
  • Willoughby Spit and Ocean View: bay-front areas with a long link to the Chesapeake Bay.
  • Ghent, Colonial Place, Larchmont, North Shore, Edgewater and Lafayette Shores: popular residential areas.
  • Downtown, Ghent and Fairmount Park: areas changed by revitalization over recent decades.

A pre-war rowhouse in Ghent, a bayside house in Ocean View and a mid-century home in Larchmont each bring different repair and flood questions. That is why a fast sale often starts with a walk-through, not a formula.

What does Norfolk's climate and flooding mean for a house?

Norfolk has a humid subtropical climate, and flooding is the main building concern. The city is low, mostly surrounded by water and slowly subsiding, and some areas already flood at high tide.

Summers are warm and humid, with 90 degree days on average 35 times a year. Winters are mild, with about 6.2 inches of snow in a typical season. The highest tropical storm risk runs from mid-August through September, when heavy rain and wind can reach the city.

The City of Norfolk publishes flood zone rules on its Flood Zones page. The Flood Insurance Rate Map from FEMA sets the zones, and the city enforces them through Article 3.9.7 of its zoning ordinance and the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code. The city lists these zones:

  • X: outside the 0.2% annual chance flood area, the least likely to flood.
  • X shaded: 0.2% annual chance, with depths under 1 foot in a 1% flood.
  • AE, AH and AO: 1% annual chance zones, with base flood elevations in AE.
  • VE: velocity zone with waves of 3 feet or more.

Norfolk runs a public tool called Forerunner where anyone can look up a property's zone and find elevation certificates. A buyer will probably check the same data, so a seller who has looked first avoids surprises.

How does the Navy and port economy affect Norfolk sellers?

Government spending, mostly military, is the largest part of Norfolk's economy. Naval Station Norfolk is the headquarters of U.S. Fleet Forces Command, which Wikipedia describes as covering more than 62,000 active-duty personnel, 75 ships and 132 aircraft. The base also hosts a NATO command.

The Virginia Port Authority is headquartered in the city and operates Norfolk International Terminals. Maersk Line, Limited and several other shipping firms have North American offices here. Sentara Health is also headquartered in Norfolk.

For sellers, this can mean timing set by orders. A military household that gets new orders may need to close in a few weeks, and a landlord with a tenant on a short lease may want out before the next rotation. Cash sales fit those schedules because there is no loan approval to wait on.

How are real estate taxes billed in Norfolk?

The City Assessor sets the value, the City Council sets the rate, and the Treasurer collects the bill. Taxes follow a July 1 to June 30 fiscal year and are paid quarterly.

  • First quarter: due September 30.
  • Second quarter: due December 5.
  • Third quarter: due March 31.
  • Fourth quarter: due June 5.

The Treasurer bills more than 68,000 taxable parcels and mails bills at least 30 days ahead. For assessment questions, call the City Assessor's Office at 757-664-4732. The Treasurer's Real Estate Tax page also lists tax relief contacts at the Department of Human Services.

The same page notes that the Treasurer collects nuisance abatement liens sent over by Neighborhood Quality, with 30 days to pay. If a Norfolk house has had weeds, trash or structure problems cleaned up by the city, ask the Treasurer for a payoff before you list or sign a contract.

Unpaid real estate tax can end in a public sale. The Treasurer's page shows an online auction held under Virginia Code 58.1-3975 in June 2026 for delinquent parcels.

What does it take to sell a Norfolk house for cash?

A cash sale in Norfolk follows the same Virginia deed rules as any other sale, but it skips the loan and the repair list. The steps are short.

  • Gather the deed, the latest tax bill and any payoff letters.
  • Check for city liens, including nuisance abatement charges.
  • Look up the flood zone on Forerunner.
  • Choose a settlement company and sign the contract.

On the deed, Virginia charges a grantor tax of 50 cents for each $500 of value, which the seller normally pays unless the contract says otherwise. The deed must show the price on its first page before the clerk will record it. Ask your settlement agent for the exact figures on your sale.

What do Norfolk sellers usually face?

Most Norfolk sellers deal with a handful of repeat problems, and the location explains many of them.

  • Water damage in crawl spaces, basements and first floors on low lots.
  • Older houses with outdated wiring, plumbing or roofs.
  • Inherited houses with several heirs and no clear next step.
  • Rental properties with tenants, deferred repairs or city notices.
  • Back taxes or city liens that need to be paid at closing.

Any of these can slow a listing, since buyers who need a loan often ask for repairs. A direct sale lets the seller pick a closing date and hand over the house as it stands.

More questions about Norfolk, VA

Is Norfolk a city or a county?

Norfolk is an independent city. It is not inside a county, so the city handles assessments, tax bills and zoning itself.

When are Norfolk real estate taxes due?

Norfolk bills quarterly, with due dates of September 30, December 5, March 31 and June 5. The fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30, according to the City Treasurer.

How do I check whether my Norfolk house is in a flood zone?

Use the city's Forerunner site, linked from the Flood Zones page. It shows the zone, flood data and any elevation certificates on file for a property.

Can I sell a Norfolk house with unpaid city liens?

Yes, but the liens are normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff on any nuisance abatement charge and the settlement agent for the rest.

Who pays the Virginia grantor tax on a Norfolk sale?

The seller pays unless the contract says the buyer will cover some or all of it. The rate is 50 cents for each $500 of value under Virginia Code 58.1-802.

Where can I ask about my Norfolk assessment?

Call the City Assessor's Office at 757-664-4732. For local permit or zoning rules that this page does not cover, ask the city office directly.

Where is Newport News, Virginia?

Newport News is an independent city on the Virginia Peninsula, along the north shore of the James River where it opens into Hampton Roads. It borders James City County, York County and Hampton by land, and shares water borders with several cities across the river.

The city covers 119.63 square miles, and 42.3 percent of that is water. Elevation averages about 15 feet. The 2020 census counted 186,247 residents and the 2025 estimate is 183,230, which makes Newport News the fifth-largest city in Virginia.

Like other Virginia cities, it has no county above it, so city offices handle assessments, tax bills and permits.

How did Newport News become one city with Warwick?

Newport News was a rural area and fishing village until the railroad arrived. In 1881 Collis P. Huntington's Peninsula Extension of the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway opened a way to bring coal to port, and a large shipyard followed within a few years. The city was incorporated in 1896.

The city annexed Kecoughtan in 1927. In 1958, voters agreed to merge Newport News with Warwick, which brought the two places back to roughly their pre-1896 footprint. That is why parts of the city still carry Warwick names.

Much of the city later grew westward, where land was available and highways were built. The older downtown went through a long decline while the shipyard and coal piers kept working.

Which Newport News neighborhoods matter to sellers?

Newport News has many distinct neighborhoods, and some sit in the former City of Warwick. Wikipedia names a long list, including these:

  • North End (Huntington Heights): developed mostly between 1900 and 1935, with many architectural styles and river views. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and the Virginia Landmarks Register.
  • Hilton Village, Denbigh, Port Warwick, Oyster Point and City Center.
  • Lee Hall: at the northwest edge, with its historic railroad station.
  • East End and Southeast: older neighborhoods near downtown and the shipyard.
  • Kiln Creek, Windsor Great Park, Newmarket Village and Riverside.

A house in the North End was built a century ago, while one in Kiln Creek is far newer. Condition, roof age and flood exposure vary between them, so any cash price should come from a look at that exact house.

What do the shipyard and military mean for the local economy?

Newport News depends on shipbuilding and the military. Newport News Shipbuilding, owned by Huntington Ingalls Industries, is the city's largest employer with more than 24,000 workers. Fort Eustis employs over 10,000 and the school system more than 5,000.

The Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility is also in the city and employs over 675 people. Ferguson Enterprises and L-3 Flight International Aviation are among the companies headquartered here, and the Newport News Marine Terminal sits at the end of the CSX rail line.

Christopher Newport University is a public university in the city, and Newport News Public Schools runs five high schools: Denbigh, Heritage, Menchville, Warwick and Woodside.

Shipyard shifts and base assignments can lead to quick moves. A worker who gets a new post or an heir who lives far away may want to close without months of showings.

How does Newport News weather affect a house?

Newport News has a humid subtropical climate with cool to mild winters and hot, humid summers. Snowfall averages 5.8 inches per season. Rain falls on about 117 days a year, and the wettest months are July, August and September.

With 42.3 percent of the city covered by water, many properties are close to the James River, creeks or low ground. Wikipedia notes that the city's position tends to be south of the usual path of northern storms and north of the usual tracks of hurricanes, but a storm can still bring heavy rain.

Sellers should ask their insurance agent for flood zone information, and pull any elevation certificate they hold, before signing a contract. The city's Geohub and the FEMA Map Service Center are places to start. Ask the city planning office about any local floodplain rule for your lot.

How are Newport News properties assessed and taxed?

The Real Estate Assessor's Office values each parcel annually, effective the following July 1. City Council decides the real estate tax rate, and the City Treasurer sends bills and collects payment.

The Assessor's Office site lists the department's authority as the Virginia Constitution, state statutes, the Newport News Charter and the city code. The office interprets laws on assessments and exemptions, publishes an annual land book and reviews assessments with owners.

This guide does not list the current tax rate or the bill due dates. Ask the Assessor or the Treasurer for the current numbers before you set a closing date, since an unpaid bill is settled from the sale proceeds.

How do people get around Newport News?

Interstate 64 is the main east and west road, and it links the city to the rest of Hampton Roads through the Hampton Roads Beltway. The Beltway crosses the harbor on two bridge-tunnels, and the Monitor-Merrimac Memorial Bridge-Tunnel is one of them. The James River Bridge also meets the city along the waterfront.

Newport News/Williamsburg International Airport lies partly inside the city. Norfolk International Airport and Richmond International Airport also serve people here. A house close to the interstate or the bridges suits commuters, though it can also mean more road noise, which a buyer may raise.

What does it take to sell a Newport News house for cash?

A cash sale in Newport News follows the same Virginia deed process as any other sale, minus lender approval. The steps are the following.

  • Collect the deed, the latest tax bill and any loan payoff letters.
  • Check the flood zone and any unpermitted work.
  • Pick a settlement company that will search title.
  • Agree on a closing date and sign.

Virginia's grantor tax is 50 cents for each $500 of value and is paid by the seller unless the parties agree otherwise. The price must appear on the first page of the deed before it can be recorded. Your settlement agent can calculate the total.

What do Newport News sellers usually face?

Sellers here run into a few repeat issues.

  • Older houses in the North End, East End or Hilton Village with aging systems.
  • Properties near water with moisture or flood concerns.
  • Rental houses with tenants and deferred repairs.
  • Inherited houses with heirs who live out of state.

A direct sale lets you skip repairs and showings and choose the date.

More questions about Newport News, VA

Is Newport News part of a county?

No. Newport News is an independent city, and it borders James City County, York County and Hampton.

Who sets the Newport News property tax rate?

City Council sets the rate. The Assessor's Office values property, and the City Treasurer sends bills and collects the tax.

How often are Newport News properties assessed?

Every parcel is assessed annually, with the value effective the following July 1, according to the Real Estate Assessor's Office.

What happened when Newport News and Warwick merged?

Voters approved a consolidation in 1958, and the combined city took the name Newport News. Some neighborhoods are still described as part of the former Warwick.

Do I need to fix my Newport News house before selling?

No. A house can be sold as is, though the buyer may price in the condition. Gather any permits and flood paperwork first, because a buyer will ask for them.

Who pays the Virginia grantor tax?

The seller does unless the contract moves it to the buyer. The rate is 50 cents per $500 of value under Virginia Code 58.1-802.

Where is Hampton, VA, and how is the city laid out?

Hampton is an independent city on the Virginia Peninsula, part of the Hampton Roads area, with no county above it. The city covers 136.27 square miles, but only 51.46 of that is land. Water makes up 62.2 percent of the total, and the average elevation is about 10 feet, according to Wikipedia's Hampton article.

That mix of rivers, creeks and Chesapeake Bay shoreline shapes almost every house sale here. Waterfront and low-lying streets sit a short drive from inland blocks that never see tidal water. A buyer, an appraiser or an insurer will treat those two kinds of property very differently.

Hampton took its present form on July 1, 1952, when the old city, the town of Phoebus and Elizabeth City County merged. The result is a city made of several older communities rather than one downtown with suburbs around it.

What is the history behind Hampton's older neighborhoods?

Hampton traces its settlement to 1610, and Hampton claims to be the oldest continuously occupied English settlement in the country. St. John's Episcopal Church, founded that year, still anchors the old town. The town was incorporated in 1705 and became a city in 1849.

Fort Monroe, at Old Point Comfort, became a place of refuge for people escaping slavery during the Civil War. The Army decommissioned the base on September 15, 2011, and it was named a National Monument on November 1 of that year. Hampton University grew out of that postwar history and sits across the Hampton River.

The neighborhoods that Wikipedia lists for the city include:

  • Aberdeen Gardens
  • Buckroe Beach
  • Farmington
  • Fox Hill
  • Hampton Woods
  • Northampton
  • Newmarket
  • Phoebus
  • Victoria Boulevard Historic District
  • Wythe, including the Olde Wythe Historic District

Houses in the historic districts can be decades or more than a century old. Older framing, original wiring and aging plumbing are common reasons a Hampton owner prefers to sell as-is instead of paying for repairs first.

Who employs people in Hampton, and does that affect a sale?

Hampton's economy leans heavily on federal aviation and research work. Langley Air Force Base is the home of the 633rd Air Base Wing and the 1st and 192nd Fighter Wings, and NASA's Langley Research Center is also in the city. Hampton University and Virginia Peninsula Community College add education jobs.

Military and federal households move on a schedule set by orders, not by the housing calendar. An owner who is transferred out of the Hampton Roads area may need to close in weeks. A sale that depends on a buyer's mortgage approval, appraisal and inspection can slip past that date.

Hampton also borders Newport News and Poquoson, and Williamsburg and Yorktown are nearby. Many residents work in a different city from the one they live in, so a house in Hampton is often judged by its commute as much as by its block.

How do roads and bridge-tunnels affect where a Hampton house sits?

Water crossings define travel here. Interstate 64 uses the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel near downtown Hampton, and Interstate 664 uses the Monitor-Merrimac Memorial Bridge-Tunnel a few miles away. The two interstates converge near the Hampton Coliseum.

Other main routes are U.S. 17, U.S. 60 and U.S. 258, plus State Routes 134 and 143. Hampton Roads Transit runs public transportation, and the Hampton Transit Center is close to downtown.

Homes close to an interstate ramp or tunnel approach tend to have shorter commutes and more road noise. Sellers should expect a buyer to ask about both.

What does the weather do to a house in Hampton?

Hampton has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and mild winters. The mean annual temperature is 60.2 degrees Fahrenheit, with about 47 inches of rain and about 6 inches of snow in an average year. The wettest month on average is August.

Moisture is the practical issue. With rainfall that high and so much surrounding water, crawl spaces, basements, roofs and drainage are the areas inspectors look at first. The temperature record runs from 105.1 degrees in August 1980 to minus 2.7 degrees in January 1985, so heating and cooling systems both get used hard.

The city's flood zone maps and any flood insurance requirement are set by the city and federal agencies. We could not open a Hampton page on that topic, so ask the city's floodplain staff or your insurer for the status of a specific address.

How are Hampton real estate taxes billed and appealed?

Hampton's city page lists the real estate tax rate at $1.14 per $100 of assessed value. The tax year runs from July 1 to June 30. The Assessor of Real Estate appraises property every year and assesses it at 100 percent of market value.

Bills for the first half are mailed around November 1 and are due December 5. Second-half bills are mailed around May 1 and are due June 5. A 10 percent penalty applies after the due date, and interest of 10 percent a year starts July 1 on unpaid balances. Confirm the current rate with the Hampton real estate tax page before you budget.

An owner who disagrees with an assessment has three steps, described on the city's appeal page:

  • Office Review: file within 30 days of the assessment notice.
  • Board of Review: file within 60 days of the notice. An office review is not required first.
  • Circuit Court: a petition can be filed without using either earlier step.

The assessor's office is at One Franklin Street, Suite 602, and the phone number is 757-727-8311. Hours are Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Where is Lynchburg, Virginia?

Lynchburg is an independent city in central Virginia, in the Blue Ridge foothills on the James River. It sits at about 630 feet of elevation and covers 49.53 square miles, nearly all of it land.

The city is bordered by Amherst County to the northeast, Bedford County to the west and northwest, and Campbell County to the south and southeast. The 2020 census counted 79,009 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 81,347, which makes Lynchburg the 11th-largest city in Virginia.

Because it is an independent city, Lynchburg has no county government above it. Assessments, tax bills and building rules all come from city offices.

Why is Lynchburg called the City of Seven Hills?

Lynchburg earned the nickname because the city spreads over seven hills: College Hill, Garland Hill, Daniel's Hill, Federal Hill, Diamond Hill, White Rock Hill and Franklin Hill. That terrain matters to a house, since steep lots mean retaining walls, long driveways and drainage runs that a flat city does not have.

John Lynch, a Quaker ferry operator, started a ferry across the James River, and the settlement grew around it after 1757. Virginia's General Assembly recognized the town in 1786, and it was incorporated as a city in 1852. Tobacco and river trade built the early economy, and Wikipedia notes that Lynchburg was the only major Virginia city not recaptured by Union forces before the Civil War ended.

What drives the Lynchburg economy?

Lynchburg is a regional hub for education and manufacturing. Wikipedia lists nuclear technology, pharmaceuticals and material handling among the industries in the metro area, and it credits many small businesses with keeping the economy stable through downturns.

Higher education is a major part of the local picture. The city is home to Liberty University, the University of Lynchburg, Randolph College, Virginia University of Lynchburg and Central Virginia Community College. Lynchburg City Public Schools serves the city, with E. C. Glass High School and Heritage High School as the two public high schools.

With several campuses in town, some Lynchburg houses are rentals. A landlord who is tired of turnover and repairs between leases can choose to sell the house as it stands.

What does Lynchburg's weather mean for a house?

Lynchburg has four seasons with cool winters and hot, humid summers. The average January temperature is 35.9 degrees and July averages 76.0 degrees, according to the 1991 to 2020 normals.

Snow averages 11.6 inches a season, and some winters are much heavier. The snowiest on record, 1995 to 1996, brought 56.8 inches. A heavy winter like that is a reminder to have the roof and heating system looked at before you sell.

The city sits along the James River. If your house is near the river or a creek, check the flood map and ask your insurance agent before you list.

The City Assessor values every parcel and sets a new value every two years. The office keeps a tax roll for July 1 through June 30 under Chapter 18-48 of the Lynchburg City Code and Title 58.1 of the Virginia Code.

The office is at 900 Church Street, Lynchburg, VA 24504, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 am to 5 pm. The phone number is 434-455-3830. The city also runs an online ParcelViewer with property details and maps.

This page does not list due dates or appeal deadlines for Lynchburg. Ask the Assessor or the Treasurer's office for the current dates, since they can change.

How do roads and rail connect Lynchburg?

Lynchburg is near the geographic center of Virginia, and its transport links are strong for a city of its size. Greater Lynchburg Transit Company runs the local bus service and the campus shuttle at Liberty University.

Kemper Street Station, at 825 Kemper Street, serves Amtrak and Greyhound. The Crescent and a Northeast Regional train stop there, and the Northeast Regional connects Lynchburg with Washington and points north. Two Norfolk Southern lines cross in the city, and CSX also has a presence.

For a seller, a house close to the station or the main bus routes can appeal to commuters and students who prefer not to drive.

  • Gather the deed, the tax bill and any payoff statements.
  • Ask the Assessor's Office about the current value on file.
  • Choose a closing date that fits your move.

Virginia puts a grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 of value on the deed, paid by the seller unless the contract shifts it. The deed must state the price on its first page to be recorded. Your settlement agent can confirm the exact charges.

  • Rental houses with turnover and unpaid repairs.

Virginia charges a grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 on the deed, and the seller usually pays it. Ask your settlement agent about any income tax question, since this page does not cover it.

The land is a rolling upland in the western part of the valley, with local relief of 100 to 300 feet. Harrisonburg has six watersheds, and Blacks Run is the primary one, with 8.67 miles of stream. How did Harrisonburg get its start?

The city was called Rocktown before it was named for Thomas Harrison, who settled in the Shenandoah Valley in 1737 and eventually claimed more than 12,000 acres near the crossing of the Spotswood Trail and the main Native American road through the valley. In 1779 he deeded 2.5 acres for a courthouse, and in 1780 he deeded 50 more acres. That land is now historic downtown Harrisonburg.

Trustees chartered a mayor and council government in 1849, and Harrisonburg became an independent city in 1916. The city today runs on a council-manager system.

The older housing stock reflects that history. Downtown has Gothic Revival churches, early twentieth century warehouses and a poultry shipping plant from 1908, and the blocks around them contain houses built across more than a century. Older homes often carry deferred maintenance, which is one reason owners choose an as-is sale.

What drives the Harrisonburg economy and housing demand?

Education is the most visible driver. James Madison University has more than 20,000 students, and Eastern Mennonite University has roughly 2,000. The housing market in a college city moves with the academic calendar, and landlords who own near campus often feel that most.

The city is also diverse. More than 1,900 refugees have been resettled in Harrisonburg since 2002, and students in the city schools speak 55 languages besides English. Rosetta Stone was founded here in 1992.

Harrisonburg City Public Schools had 6,830 students in kindergarten through grade 12 in fall 2024. It runs six elementary schools, two middle schools and two high schools:

  • High schools: Harrisonburg High School and Rocktown High School
  • Middle schools: Skyline Middle School and Thomas Harrison Middle School
  • Elementary schools: Bluestone, Smithland, Spotswood, Stone Spring, Waterman and W.H. Keister

Private options include Eastern Mennonite School, Blue Ridge Christian School and Redeemer Classical School.

What is the climate like, and what does it do to a house?

Harrisonburg has a humid subtropical climate with four distinct seasons: hot, humid summers and cool to cold winters. It sits in USDA hardiness zone 6b, where average winter lows run from minus 5 to 0 degrees Fahrenheit.

Winter lows of that kind put stress on plumbing in unheated spaces, on roofs and on older heating systems. A buyer's inspector will look at the furnace and the attic first. A seller who already knows the age of the system can answer quickly and avoid a late price renegotiation.

The city also offers tax relief for the elderly and disabled and an exemption for disabled veterans. Ask the Commissioner of the Revenue whether a property qualifies. Anyone who moves should give the Commissioner a new billing address, because bills go to the last address on record.

In a city with two universities, a few situations come up again and again.

A tenant in place complicates a traditional listing, because showings need notice and some buyers want vacant possession. A cash buyer can often take over a house with tenants, but the lease terms still apply. Share the lease early so the offer reflects it.

A cash sale removes the buyer's loan, so the schedule is controlled by title work and your own paperwork. You describe the house, the buyer reviews it, and a written offer follows. If you accept, a title or settlement company searches for liens and prepares the closing.

Bring any bills that affect the closing, such as the December 5 or June 5 tax installment, plus the deed and, for an estate, proof of who may sign. Choosing the closing date is up to you within what the title search allows.

Before you accept any offer, put the numbers side by side. Add up what a listing would cost in repairs, agent fees and months of carrying costs such as taxes, utilities and insurance, then compare that to the net from a cash sale. Harrisonburg's twice-a-year tax schedule makes carrying costs easy to forget, so count at least one installment if the house may sit through a bill date.

The city adds a late penalty of 10 percent with a $10 minimum, and annual interest of 10 percent starts January 1 or July 1 depending on the half.

What is Leesburg's history, and why does it matter to a seller?

The Virginia General Assembly founded Leesburg on October 12, 1758, on 60 acres laid out by Nicholas Minor in six crossing streets. During the War of 1812 the town sheltered federal documents, including the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, when Washington was threatened.

Early in the Civil War the Battle of Ball's Bluff was fought about 2 miles northeast of the town center, and Leesburg changed hands several times. The Leesburg historic district was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1970.

How did Leesburg change from a rural town to a commuter hub?

Leesburg went from 1,703 residents in 1950 to 16,202 in 1990, 28,311 in 2000 and 42,616 in 2010. The 2020 census counted 48,250. Wikipedia describes the change as a move from a small rural Piedmont town to a suburban community for commuters to the capital.

Growth concentrates along the Dulles Greenway and State Route 7. The housing stock therefore ranges from nineteenth century downtown houses to subdivisions built in the last several decades, and those two kinds of houses sell on very different terms.

  • Loudoun Medical Group: 100 to 250

The FAA's Washington Air Route Traffic Control Center is in Leesburg. Leesburg Executive Airport at Godfrey Field is a reliever airport for Dulles, and a 2011 state study put its economic impact at nearly $78 million a year.

Who lives in Leesburg, and what green space is nearby?

The median age in the 2020 census was 35.6. About 26.8 percent of residents were under 18 and 9.4 percent were 65 or older. Of 16,184 households, 42.4 percent had children, and 57.7 percent were married-couple households. The homeowner vacancy rate was 0.6 percent and the rental vacancy rate was 4.8 percent.

Parks shape how neighborhoods feel. Ida Lee Park grew from a 141-acre farm donated to the town in 1986. Morven Park is a 1,000-acre historic estate and horse park. Annual events include the Flower and Garden Festival in April, a Fourth of July parade, a classic car show on the first Saturday in June, an airshow on the last Saturday in September and a long-running Halloween parade.

U.S. Route 15, State Route 7 and State Route 267 serve the town. Route 15 and Route 7 meet on the Leesburg Bypass, and Route 267, the Dulles Greenway, ends at the bypass. Have the deed, your mortgage payoff information and any estate paperwork ready. A consolidated county and town tax bill makes the tax part of closing simpler, because there is only one account to check.

Ask any buyer for the offer in writing, confirm who pays for title and settlement charges, and read the closing statement before you sign. If a family member must approve the sale, bring them into the conversation before an offer arrives, so the closing date is not held up by a signature.

Where is Manassas, Virginia?

Manassas is a small independent city in Northern Virginia, and it is the county seat of Prince William County. It is separate from the county, and it borders the independent city of Manassas Park.

The city covers 9.9 square miles at an elevation of about 305 feet. The 2020 census counted 42,772 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 44,332. Manassas is part of the Washington-Arlington-Alexandria metropolitan area.

Because Manassas is an independent city, it does not use county offices for assessments or tax bills. The city's own Commissioner of the Revenue and Treasurer handle them.

What is the history of Manassas?

Manassas began as a railroad stop and became a junction in the early 1860s. A post office and a stop on the Orange and Alexandria Railroad opened in 1851 in the area called Tudor Hall, and the Manassas Gap Railroad reached Strasburg by 1854.

Two Civil War battles were fought nearby: the First Battle of Bull Run in July 1861 and the Second in August 1862. After the war, the crossroads grew into a town that was incorporated in 1873. Manassas became the Prince William county seat in 1894, and it incorporated as an independent city in 1975.

Several historic sites remain, including the Manassas Historic District, Liberia plantation house, the Manassas Water Tower, Cannon Branch Fort and Annaburg. The city bought Annaburg in July 2019 to restore it as a public park.

What is the housing like in Manassas?

Manassas has an older core and a lot of housing from the 1980s. Wikipedia notes that 35 percent of the city's housing stock was built between 1980 and 1989, the city's highest period of growth. That figure comes from a source about a decade old, so treat it as a rough guide.

The 2020 census found 13,983 households, and 39.8 percent of them had children under 18. The homeowner vacancy rate was 0.7 percent and the rental vacancy rate was 3.3 percent, so few homes sat empty. About 26 percent of residents were under 18.

Old Town Manassas is the historic center, with First Friday events on the first Friday of each month. The city has 260 acres of parkland.

A house from that decade is now around 40 years old, so roofs, heating and cooling systems and water heaters may be due for replacement. A buyer's inspector will look at those items.

  • Intermediate: Baldwin and Mayfield, for fifth and sixth grade.
  • Middle: Grace E. Metz. High: Osbourn High School.

Some Prince William County schools have Manassas mailing addresses but sit outside the city limits, so a Manassas address does not always mean the city school district. Check the district for any address.

If your lender collects taxes through escrow, the Treasurer notes that your bill is probably paid by the mortgage company. The office does not send copies to homeowners, so a person with escrow should pass any bill received on to the lender.

Residents aged 65 or older and certain disabled people may qualify for exemption or deferral through Tax Relief. Delinquent accounts may be handed to a collection firm. Under Virginia law, not getting a bill does not remove penalty and interest.

Questions about collection go to 703-257-8241. City Hall is at 9027 Center Street. This guide does not list the current rate, so ask the city.

Virginia charges a grantor tax of 50 cents for each $500 of value, which the seller pays unless the contract says the buyer will. The deed must state the price on its first page before the clerk can record it. Ask your settlement agent for the final figures, and check with the city for any local rule about your property.

Where is Herndon, VA, and is it a town or a city?

Herndon is an incorporated town in Fairfax County, in Northern Virginia and the Washington, D.C. metro area. It covers 4.29 square miles at an elevation of about 361 feet, and the 2020 census counted 24,655 residents, according to Wikipedia. It is the largest of the three incorporated towns in the county.

A town in Virginia sits inside a county, so Herndon owners deal with two governments. The town runs its own council and its own police department, while Fairfax County handles assessment and tax billing. A little over two acres of the town technically lie in Loudoun County.

How did Herndon develop?

The settlement took the name Herndon in 1858, after naval officer William Lewis Herndon, who died with his ship, the SS Central America, while helping save more than 150 passengers and crew. Many Northern soldiers and families settled here in the 1870s, drawn by the climate and low land prices.

The area grew as a dairy and vacation hub along the Alexandria, Loudoun and Hampshire Railroad, later the Washington and Old Dominion Railroad. The old line is now the W&OD hike and bike trail, and the train station has become the Herndon Depot Museum. The Herndon Historic District is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

Population growth came late. Herndon had 1,960 people in 1960 and 11,449 in 1980, then reached 24,655 in 2020. Most of the town's growth came after 1960, so many houses are from the later twentieth century, with older ones near the historic downtown.

Who are the largest employers in Herndon?

Herndon is part of the Dulles Technology Corridor, and its largest employers are technology and government contractors. Wikipedia reports the principal employers from the town's 2025 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report:

  • Amazon Web Services, Karsun Solutions, Northwest Federal Credit Union, Peraton and Boeing: 250 to 499 each
  • Town of Herndon, Smartronix, Everfox Holdings and Allwyn: 100 to 249 each

The 2022 American Community Survey figures cited on the same page put median household income in the town at $133,403, and 52.5 percent of residents held a bachelor's degree or higher. Wikipedia also notes that 53.7 percent of residents spoke a language other than English at home.

For a seller, the practical effect is a buyer pool that includes contractors and government workers who can be sensitive to a job change or a security clearance timeline. Those sellers may need to close fast when a relocation arrives.

How do roads and the Metro affect a Herndon address?

State Route 228 runs through the center of town along Elden Street, Monroe Street, Park Avenue and Dranesville Road. A truck route follows Herndon Parkway around downtown. At the south end of town, Route 228 meets State Route 267, the Dulles Toll Road, which leads to Washington via Interstate 66 and to Dulles International Airport.

How are Herndon real estate taxes billed?

The due dates are July 28 for the first installment and December 5 for the second. Late balances carry additional penalties and interest. The Fairfax County Department of Tax Administration answers assessment and payment questions at (703) 222-8234 or DTARED@fairfaxcounty.gov, and it also runs the tax relief program. Because two installments land in July and December, a closing near either date should account for who pays the bill that is due. Your title company can prorate it.
